title: How can one reusable address receive payments at fresh outputs?
dek: Publish an address once. Receive at fresh outputs. Your wallet does the work of finding which payments belong to you.

blocks.text: An address is easy to put on a website and awkward to keep using. When every payment goes to that same address, an observer can group the payments together. Giving each sender a fresh address avoids that pattern, but now you have to supply addresses whenever someone wants to pay.

Silent payments let you publish a reusable address while senders pay to fresh Taproot outputs. The address gives them what they need to calculate those outputs. Your wallet can calculate them too, using its scanning key and information in each transaction. That is how it finds your money without a separate notification.

figure.title: One address to publish; a payment to find
figure.caption: The public address helps the sender create a payment. The receiver uses its private scan key to recognise the resulting output.

blocks.text: Begin with a simpler version of the idea. Alice wants to pay Bob. She has a private key and Bob’s public key; Bob has his private key and can see Alice’s public key in her transaction. Each combines the private key they hold with the public key of the other person.

Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman makes those two calculations reach the same point. Alice and Bob arrive there from different directions. Someone watching with only the public keys cannot perform the same calculation under the usual Diffie–Hellman assumption. The secret is computed at each end, rather than sent between them.

blocks.title: Different keys, the same destination
blocks.caption: The simplified exchange: Alice computes a·B, Bob computes b·A, and both reach S.

blocks.text: Alice hashes that shared point and uses the result to tweak Bob’s public key. The tweaked key is where she pays. Bob can repeat the calculation and look for that key among the transaction’s outputs. Finding a match tells him which output to spend, and he can apply the corresponding tweak to his private spending key.

An observer sees the transaction too. What they lack is the private information needed to reproduce the shared secret and connect that output to Bob’s address. The output itself is an ordinary Taproot output. The authors want silent payments to blend in with other transactions, without extra on-chain notification data.

The idea is elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman. If Alice holds the private key a for public key A, and Bob holds b for B, then a·B and b·A are the same point. In BIP 352’s simple case, Alice pays Bob at P = B + hash(a·B)·G. Bob sees A in Alice’s transaction, computes hash(b·A) himself, and looks for P among the outputs. Under the usual Diffie–Hellman assumption, anyone without a or b cannot compute that hash, so cannot connect P to B.

There is no public tag saying “for Bob.” His wallet has to inspect transactions that could contain silent payments and try the calculation. That work moves to the receiver so that the sender can pay without first asking for a new address.

A payment may include several outputs for the same receiver. The calculation therefore includes a counter. Bob starts with P₀. If that output is present, he tries P₁, then keeps going until the first missing output. In the example below, two outputs match and the next does not.

blocks.title: Find a match, then try the next
blocks.caption: P₀ and P₁ are present. P₂ is absent, so this search stops.

blocks.text: Stopping at a gap has a consequence for the sender. Every generated output MUST appear in the finished transaction. If the sender removed P₁ but kept P₂, Bob would stop at the missing P₁ and never discover the later payment. Output discovery depends on this shared ordering.

Scanning is also the main cost of the design. BIP 352’s authors describe it as generally feasible for full nodes and challenging for light clients. Their appendix explores ways a light client might use extra transaction data and block filters, but that discussion is outside the specification.

blocks.summary: Which transactions to scan and when to stop

blocks.text: Nothing on chain tells Bob a payment has arrived. For silent payments v0, a transaction MUST be scanned if and only if it has at least one taproot output, at least one eligible input, and spends no output with a SegWit version above 1. For each such transaction Bob sums the input keys, computes the input hash and the shared secret, and checks the taproot outputs for P_0.

If P_0 is there, he checks for P_1, and so on; at the first one not found, he stops. These extra checks happen only after a match, so the authors call the added cost negligible. Since version 1.1.0 the search is also capped: a sender fails if any group of recipient addresses sharing one scan key is larger than K_max = 2323, and a receiver stops at k = 2323, which the changelog says mitigates quadratic scanning on adversarial transactions.

The full address carries two public keys. One is the scan key, which helps find incoming payments. The other is the spend key, which controls spending. Their private counterparts can be kept in different places: scanning can happen online while the spending key remains in cold storage.

This separation matters during ordinary use. A wallet needs to keep checking for receipts; it need not bring the spending key online every time it does so. A scanning setup has private information of its own, but that information does not by itself give it the spending key.

The address is a set of public instructions for deriving outputs, rather than the output key of a particular coin. For version 0 on mainnet it is 116 characters long and starts sp1q. The two compressed public keys account for 66 bytes inside it. The address uses Bech32m to encode them and detect errors.

Labels let Bob distinguish receipts while continuing to scan with the same key. A labeled address changes the spending side and keeps the scan key. That is convenient bookkeeping, but anyone comparing those addresses can see their shared scan key and tell that they belong together.

blocks.title: Different labels, the same receiver
blocks.caption: The shared scan key links these published addresses. Labels distinguish receipts; they do not create separate identities.

blocks.text: Labels let Bob tell payments apart without scanning for several addresses. He publishes (B_scan, B_m), where B_m = B_spend + hash(b_scan ‖ m)·G. When an output does not match P_k directly, he subtracts P_k and checks whether the difference is one of his label points; if not, he negates the output and tries again, because an x-only output does not say which y it had. Label m = 0 is reserved for change: the BIP stresses that a wallet never hands it out, and says every receiving wallet should at least scan for it when recovering from backup.

sections.heading: Make each payment depend on its transaction

blocks.text: The simple Alice-and-Bob exchange leaves out a practical detail: a transaction can have several inputs. The full protocol adds together the keys from all eligible inputs before computing the shared secret. Sender and receiver must choose exactly the same keys, or they will calculate different destinations.

An additional hash ties the calculation to the smallest outpoint and the combined input public key. That makes the destination depend on which coins are being spent, so paying again from the same keys does not simply reuse the previous output. The receiver can recover this input information from the transaction.

Only certain input types provide the needed keys in a suitable form. BIP 352 excludes inputs with several keys or conditional branches from the shared-secret calculation: they would let a sender re-sign with a different set of public keys after the output was derived, a problem in collaborative transactions. It also requires at least one eligible input. Funding a payment and contributing a key to its calculation are distinct jobs.

blocks.title: Which inputs contribute a key?
blocks.caption: Some inputs can help fund the transaction without contributing to the shared secret. The marks show which keys enter the calculation.

blocks.text: The interactive example brings those pieces together. Follow the sender’s calculation, then switch to the receiver. Finally inspect the observer’s view. Both participants can recognise the payment; the public transaction alone does not provide the secret used to connect it to the address.

blocks.title: The same payment, three viewpoints
blocks.caption: Switch between sender, receiver and observer. Each view shows only the information available on that side.

blocks.summary: The full derivation, including the counter

blocks.text: The shared secret is input_hash·a·B_scan on Alice’s side and input_hash·b_scan·A on Bob’s; they are the same point. From it Alice derives t_k, a tagged hash of the secret and a counter k, and pays to P_k = B_spend + t_k·G (B_m in place of B_spend for a labeled address), starting with k = 0 and adding one for each further output to the same receiver. To spend, Bob uses b_spend + t_k (plus the label tweak, for a labeled output), mod n, as the private key.

Not every input contributes to the secret. Any UTXO with a known output script can fund the transaction (though the sender leaves out outputs with a SegWit version above 1), but sender and receiver MUST derive the shared secret only from inputs of four types: P2TR, P2WPKH, P2SH-P2WPKH and P2PKH. For each, the receiver has to find the public key in what the transaction reveals: the last witness item for the two P2WPKH forms, the scriptSig for P2PKH, and the taproot output key itself for P2TR.

Inputs with conditional branches or several keys, such as CHECKMULTISIG, are left out; the BIP explains that they would let a participant in a collaborative transaction re-sign with different keys after the output was derived. Only compressed and x-only keys count, so an input that reveals an uncompressed key is skipped. A taproot script-path spend still counts, through its output key: the sender MUST hold that key’s private key or leave the input out, unless the internal key is the NUMS point H from BIP 341, in which case the input is skipped.

Two details keep sender and receiver in step. A taproot key is x-only, and the receiver assumes the even-y point when it sums the keys, so the sender negates any taproot private key whose point has odd y. And for P2PKH, the receiver MUST parse the scriptSig for the key even when it does not match the usual template, because a third party can malleate a P2PKH scriptSig.
A transaction with no eligible input has no secret at all, so a sender’s coin selection MUST include at least one.

The sender has rules of its own. It should sign with DEFAULT, ALL, SINGLE or NONE; the BIP calls ANYONECANPAY unsafe. And every output it generated MUST appear in the final transaction: if P_1 were dropped, the receiver, stopping at the first gap, would never find P_2.

sections.heading: What you still have to look after

blocks.text: Reusing the public address removes one source of on-chain links. It does not make every surrounding choice private. Labeled addresses can still be grouped together, and the authors advise that a transaction’s inputs belong to one entity: they do not claim a formal security proof for collaborative use.

Backups need thought as well. A wallet restored from its seed can rebuild its history by scanning from its birthday. Because outputs are derived individually, the BIP also recommends regular backups. The convenience of a permanent receiving address comes with a wallet that must remember how to search.

BIP 352 was assigned in 2023 and is recorded as Complete in the pinned source. The examples use its published send-and-receive vectors. The receiver’s scanning rule includes a bound, K_max = 2323, added in version 1.1.0.
